questions.q: Mechanical ocular trauma is divided into blunt trauma and:
questions.exp: The mechanical-trauma diagram divides injury into blunt (closed-globe injuries/contusions) and penetrating trauma. (Book p220)

questions.q: Which is an example of blunt ocular trauma listed on the page?
questions.exp: Blunt-trauma examples include injury by fist, tennis ball and champagne cork. (Book p220)

questions.q: Match the sign with its description — 1) Black eye  2) Subconjunctival hemorrhage … A) Periocular hematoma  B) Common in trivial trauma
questions.exp: Black eye is periocular hematoma; subconjunctival hemorrhage is common in trivial trauma. (Book p220)

questions.q: The most common sign of blunt ocular trauma is blood in the anterior chamber, called:
questions.exp: Hyphema is a collection of blood in the anterior chamber and is listed as the most common sign of blunt ocular trauma. (Book p220)

questions.q: The bleeding source in traumatic hyphema is the:
questions.exp: The source of bleeding is given as the circulus arteriosus major. (Book p220)

questions.q: Which is the listed reason for topical steroids in hyphema, with atropine as an optional adjunct?
opts: To prevent rebleeding and associated inflammation
To lower the risk of siderosis
questions.exp: Topical steroids are used to prevent rebleeding and associated inflammation; atropine is optional. (Book p220)

questions.q: If hyphema has not resorbed by ___ days, anterior-chamber paracentesis/washing is considered.
questions.exp: Paracentesis/washing is listed if there is no resorption until 4 days. (Book p220)

questions.q: Match the iris injury — 1) Iridodonesis  2) Iridodialysis … A) Detachment of iris root from ciliary body  B) Tremulous iris
questions.exp: Iridodonesis is tremulous iris; iridodialysis is detachment of the iris root from ciliary body and produces a D-shaped pupil. (Book p220)

questions.q: A D-shaped pupil after blunt trauma points to:
questions.exp: Iridodialysis detaches the iris root from the ciliary body and is associated with a D-shaped pupil. (Book p220)

questions.q: Which traumatic lens-sign set is correctly matched?
opts: Rosette cataract: nuclear; Vossius ring: posterior lens imprint
Rosette cataract: cortical; Vossius ring: iris-root tear
Rosette cataract: anterior subcapsular; Vossius ring: vitreous pigment
Rosette cataract: posterior subcapsular; Vossius ring: miotic-pupil imprint on anterior lens
questions.exp: Rosette-shaped cataract is posterior subcapsular; Vossius ring is the imprint of a miotic pupil on the anterior lens surface. (Book p220)

questions.q: The most common cause of ectopia lentis/subluxation listed here is:
questions.exp: Ectopia lentis or subluxation of the lens is most commonly caused by blunt trauma. (Book p220)

questions.q: Phacodonesis refers to a ___ lens.
questions.exp: Phacodonesis is a tremulous lens. (Book p220)

questions.q: Match the posterior-segment sign — 1) Berlin edema  2) Commotio retinae … A) Cloudy grey appearance  B) Fluid collection after blunt trauma
questions.exp: Berlin edema is fluid collection due to blunt trauma; commotio retinae has a cloudy grey appearance. (Book p221)

questions.q: Traumatic optic neuropathy is described on this page as:
questions.exp: The page characterizes traumatic optic neuropathy as self-limiting. (Book p221)

questions.q: A choroidal rupture may have a ___-handle configuration.
questions.exp: The listed configuration of choroidal rupture is bucket-handle. (Book p221)

questions.q: After falling on a knob-like object, globe rupture is suspected. The common site listed is the superonasal limbus near:
questions.exp: Globe rupture may follow a fall on a knob-like object; the listed site is superonasal limbus near Schlemm canal. (Book p221)

questions.q: Penetrating trauma may lead to sympathetic ophthalmia, a:
questions.exp: Sympathetic ophthalmia (panuveitis) and intraocular foreign body are listed complications of penetrating trauma. (Book p221)

questions.q: For suspected metallic intraocular foreign body, match investigation and contraindicated imaging — IOC: ___; contraindicated: ___.
questions.exp: Iron and steel are common IOFBs; CT is the investigation of choice and MRI is contraindicated. (Book p221)

questions.q: Iron deposition in the eye produces which named condition and associated findings?
opts: Chalcosis with sunflower cataract and hypotony
Siderosis bulbi with lens-capsule rust ring, iris hyperpigmentation and secondary open-angle glaucoma
questions.exp: Siderosis bulbi follows iron deposition and may cause a rust ring on anterior lens capsule, iris hyperpigmentation and secondary open-angle glaucoma. (Book p221)

questions.q: Which reaction is used to stain iron deposits in siderosis bulbi?
questions.exp: The diagnostic Prussian blue reaction stains iron deposits. (Book p221)

questions.q: Uveitis after contact with caterpillar hair is called:
questions.exp: Ophthalmia nodosa is associated with caterpillar-hair contact and uveitis. (Book p221)

questions.q: The most common orbital fracture in trauma is a blow-out fracture of the orbital:
questions.exp: A blow-out fracture involves the orbital floor and is the most common orbital fracture in trauma. (Book p221)

questions.q: Blow-out fracture with inferior oblique/inferior rectus entrapment causes restrictive diplopia on:
questions.exp: Clinical findings include infraorbital nerve anaesthesia and restrictive diplopia; entrapped inferior oblique/inferior rectus cause diplopia in upgaze and downgaze. (Book p221)

questions.q: The X-ray sign associated with orbital fracture is the:
questions.exp: The orbital-trauma investigation note labels the X-ray tear-drop sign. (Book p222)

questions.q: Raccoon or panda eyes after trauma suggest fracture of the orbital:
questions.exp: Fracture of the roof of the orbit presents with raccoon/panda eyes. (Book p222)

questions.q: Match the chemical with its tissue effect — 1) Alkali  2) Acid … A) Coagulation, limited penetration  B) Necrosis, deeper penetration
questions.exp: Alkali causes tissue necrosis and deeper penetration; acid causes coagulation and does not penetrate as deeply. (Book p222)

questions.q: Which two classifications are listed for grading ocular-surface burns?
questions.exp: Dua and Roper-Hall classifications are listed for grading ocular surface burns. (Book p222)

questions.q: The immediate first-aid management of chemical eye injury is:
opts: Copious irrigation with BSS/Ringer lactate, with double eversion of the eyelids
questions.exp: Management begins with copious irrigation using balanced salt solution or Ringer lactate and double eversion of eyelids. (Book p222)

questions.q: Match the adjunct in chemical injury — 1) Atropine  2) Topical sodium citrate … A) Prevents proteolysis  B) Relieves ciliary spasm
questions.exp: Listed treatment includes topical antibiotics, atropine for ciliary spasm, lubricants and topical sodium citrate to prevent proteolysis. (Book p222)

units.title: Blunt ocular trauma
units.guide: Blunt trauma causes closed-globe injury and contusion. Recognize hyphema, iris/lens signs and their named features; manage hyphema to prevent rebleeding and intervene for persistent blood.

units.title: Posterior-segment, penetrating and orbital trauma
units.guide: Blunt trauma may produce retinal, choroidal or globe injury. Penetrating trauma raises concern for sympathetic ophthalmia and IOFB; iron IOFB causes siderosis. Blow-out and roof fractures have distinctive findings.

units.title: Chemical ocular injuries
units.guide: Alkali burns penetrate deeply after liquefactive necrosis; acids cause coagulation and less penetration. Grade ocular-surface burns with Dua or Roper-Hall and begin immediate copious irrigation, followed by supportive and anti-proteolytic treatment.
